parts.note: places where students go to study books are named for a Berkshire town plus a word for apartments

explanation.walkthrough: READING is the county town of Berkshire ('Berks'), and ROOMS are apartments; together they name the library rooms where students read.
explanation.definitionFit: Libraries and similar halls set aside for quiet study are where students sit with their books.

definitions.meaning: someone who makes a soft swishing sound rather than a racket, a loud din

explanation.walkthrough: 'racketeer' looks like a gangster, but here it means one who makes a racket (noise); a rustler makes only a soft rustle.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustler steals livestock; and one who rustles makes a quiet sound, not a din.

definitions.meaning: sizes of surfaces, in square units
the sunken yards in front of basements

explanation.walkthrough: In British houses an area is the sunken courtyard in front of a basement; the surface suggests lower law courts.
explanation.definitionFit: Square measurements of surfaces; and sunken basement yards below street level.

clue.text: I will go'; nett rise is dis: honestly obtained

parts.note: contracted, I will becomes I'll
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the word nett is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone leaving remarks that a rise in net earnings was crookedly come by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rise' turns NETT upwards into TTEN in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill-gotten gains are those acquired by crooked or unlawful means.

indicators.note: sounds signals that the word is spoken and we hear its sound-alike

parts.note: a Gael is a Celt of Scotland or Ireland

explanation.surface: A woman has a Celtic-sounding voice or name.
explanation.walkthrough: The name Gail sounds the same as Gael, a Gaelic-speaking Celt.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name, so a woman can be called 'she'.

parts.note: overt means done openly, not hidden
an urn is a tall vase

explanation.surface: Knocking over an open vase spills its contents.
explanation.definitionFit: To upset or tip over something so it falls, as a spilt cup does.

parts.note: a police van carrying arrested people is called Black plus a girl's name

explanation.walkthrough: A Black Maria is British slang for a police van that collects prisoners; Maria is also a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The girl's name that, after Black, is the slang for a police prisoner van.

parts.note: a bar is a pub or drinking place
gains are profits

explanation.surface: A pub's profits are made at little cost.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods bought below their worth are cheap buys, acquired at low cost.

clue.text: Signal' to stop horseplay maddens' certain speculators

parts.note: a red light or flag tells traffic to stop
a rag is a boisterous student prank or horseplay

explanation.surface: A warning to halt rough play annoys a group of investors.
explanation.walkthrough: Bulls are stock-market speculators betting on rising prices; a red rag is said to madden a bull.
explanation.definitionFit: Waving red cloth is said to enrage a bull, and bulls are speculators on rising shares.

clue.text: Bombardment goes South to Dashwood's Club

indicators.note: the first piece goes up to the second, placed in front of it
the first piece goes up to the second, placed in front of it

parts.note: Sir Francis Dashwood founded the eighteenth-century Hellfire Club

explanation.surface: An artillery barrage is aimed southwards at a gentlemen's club run by Dashwood.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hellfire Club was a notorious eighteenth-century English society of rakes founded by Sir Francis Dashwood.
explanation.definitionFit: Artillery shells raining down on a target make up a bombardment.

clue.text: It 'is never too late to mend Charles

definitions.text: It 'is never too late to mend Charles

parts.words: It 'is never too late to mend Charles
parts.note: the title of a Victorian novel followed by its author's first name

explanation.walkthrough: 'It Is Never Too Late to Mend' (1856) is a novel by the Victorian writer Charles Reade; the clue reads like a proverb about a man named Charles.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist who wrote that 1856 book about prison reform was Charles of that surname.

clue.text: Instruction one has in hot weather'

definitions.meaning: a piece of teaching, a class
split in two, the letters say that in a heatwave one wears fewer clothes

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer as LESS ON: in hot weather one has less on.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesson is a period of teaching; and in summer heat a person wears less clothing.

parts.note: a Ranger was a senior member of the Girl Guides, so a guide

explanation.surface: A street guide turns out to be from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Rangers were the senior section of the Girl Guides in Britain; a ranger can also be a park guide.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from another country is an outsider, unknown to the locals.

clue.text: This will perhaps be rate of deduction

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the following letters may be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: Someone muses that this may be the rate at which a deduction is made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' tells you to rearrange the letters of BE RATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebate is money knocked off a bill or refunded, a reduction in the amount owed.

parts.note: best means the finest
a ride is a horse or mount for riding

explanation.surface: Someone gets up on the best horse available.
explanation.definitionFit: To bestride a horse is to sit astride it, to get on and sit it.

parts.note: the Cree are a Native American (Indian) people
a ping is a short ringing sound

explanation.surface: A gentle passage of music played on an Indian instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indian' here means a Native American people, the Cree, not someone from India.
explanation.definitionFit: Inching along stealthily is the act of crawling forward slowly.

parts.note: the pupil is the dark centre of the eye, standing for the whole eye
bright means shining

explanation.surface: A herbal remedy is said to make a schoolchild's eyes sparkle.
explanation.walkthrough: Euphrasia is the botanical name of a small meadow plant once used to treat eye complaints.
explanation.definitionFit: Euphrasia is the Latin genus name of a small wild flower used in folk medicine for sore eyes.

definitions.meaning: set at large, freed from captivity (an old sense)

explanation.walkthrough: An old sense of the word meant set at large, released from prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Released from confinement, in an archaic sense; and made bigger or expanded.

indicators.note: saying something is wrong signals that these letters are in the wrong order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a sound came from the stern of a ship and is told no.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's wrong' tells you to rearrange the letters of ASTERN plus NO.
explanation.definitionFit: A resonant voice rings and reverberates, as an echo does.

parts.note: rep is a ribbed fabric used for upholstery
a programme being broadcast on radio is on air

explanation.surface: Someone praises good-quality cloth heard about on a radio show.
explanation.definitionFit: To fix or mend something is to restore it to working order.

parts.note: Soviet Russia was called Red

explanation.walkthrough: In the Cold War, 'Red' meant Communist; Russia long wanted a warm-water sea such as the Mediterranean, so its dream would be a 'Red sea'.
explanation.definitionFit: The body of water between Africa and Arabia, joined to the Mediterranean by the Suez Canal.

parts.note: the grave is one of the marks placed over vowels in French, so these are examples

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grave' suggests solemn omens, but it is the grave mark over a vowel, as in French à.
explanation.definitionFit: Grave, acute and circumflex are all marks written over letters to show pronunciation.

clue.text: Apparent displacement when gunners hold everything in plea for peace

indicators.note: the gunners with what they hold are placed in the middle of the word for peace

parts.note: pax is Latin for peace, called out as a plea for a truce

indicators.note: the gunners hold everything, so the word all sits inside the gunners' letters

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, the gunners
all means everything

explanation.surface: Artillerymen grasping everything while pleading for peace seem to shift position.
explanation.walkthrough: PAX is a schoolchild's call for a truce in Britain. 'hold' puts ALL inside RA (Royal Artillery), giving RALLA; 'in' sets that inside PAX.
explanation.definitionFit: Parallax is the way an object seems to shift against its background when seen from two different points.

clue.text: Yarn that brings: money to the island

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound (libra), so money
an isle is an island

explanation.surface: A tall story about bringing money to an island.
explanation.walkthrough: L stands for the pound sterling, from Latin libra.
explanation.definitionFit: Lisle is a fine, strong cotton thread, used for stockings.

parts.note: someone who reviews plays, comedies included, and gives a verdict on them

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone presiding over a funny court case; it means a reviewer who assesses comic plays.
explanation.definitionFit: A reviewer who assesses and pronounces on stage works, including comedies.

parts.note: taken as written
ME is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Maine

explanation.surface: A breath of fresh air in the state of Maine.
explanation.definitionFit: A tune's main melody, the subject of a piece of music.

indicators.note: done anyhow, any old way, so the letters are put in a random order

explanation.surface: A man named Jacobson might be alive one way or another.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Jacobson' as 'Jacob's son': Levi was a son of Jacob in Genesis. 'anyhow' rearranges LIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, Levi is the third son born to Jacob and Leah.

clue.text: Try hard work on this river .

indicators.note: the word try goes on after the river's name to make hard work, so taking it off hard work leaves the river

parts.note: industry means diligent hard work
taken as written

explanation.surface: A command to make a real effort on a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Put TRY on after this river and you get INDUSTRY, 'hard work'; so the river is INDUSTRY without TRY.
explanation.definitionFit: The great river of Pakistan, rising in Tibet and flowing to the Arabian Sea.

parts.note: Lady Jane Grey was the nine-days queen of England in 1553
green with envy, so green means jealous

explanation.surface: Lady Jane is envious of someone's complexion.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Jane Grey was briefly Queen of England in 1553 before being executed.
explanation.definitionFit: A shade between grey and green is a hue, a kind of colouring.

definitions.meaning: the post of chief lover to the great seducer

explanation.walkthrough: A principal is the head of a school; Casanova, the famous lover, would have a chief or 'head' mistress among his girlfriends.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who runs a girls' school; and, split, the top lover of a famous womaniser.
